readingInstruction: Read Proverbs 28:1-29:27. These chapters are about leadership, justice, and the effect of rulers on a nation. Notice what they say about confession, and the fear of man.
settingTheScene: These chapters continue the collection copied by Hezekiah’s men. The focus turns to rulers and the righteous. They reflect the concern for justice that runs through the prophets. The wise sayings here are strongly moral and contrast the righteous with the wicked, the oppressor with the generous, and the stubborn with the repentant.
observation: “The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold as a lion” (28:1).
“Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy” (28:13).
“Blessed is the one who fears the LORD always, but whoever hardens his heart will fall into calamity” (28:14).
“Whoever trusts in his own mind is a fool, but he who walks in wisdom will be delivered” (28:26).
“Whoever gives to the poor will not want, but he who hides his eyes will get many a curse” (28:27).
“When the righteous increase, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan” (29:2).
“Where there is no prophecy the people cast off restraint, but blessed is he who keeps the law” (29:18).
“The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe” (29:25).
interpretation:
The first verse of chapter 28 describes a mark of conscience. The wicked run when no one is chasing them, because guilt is its own pursuer. The righteous are bold, because they have nothing to hide. A clear conscience is a source of courage.

Verse 13 is one of the central statements on confession in the Bible: “Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy.” Both confession and forsaking are required. It is not enough to admit a sin and carry on. And the promise is mercy. David knew this from his own experience (Psalm 32). Hiding sin makes things worse. Confessing opens the way to mercy.

Verse 26 returns to the theme of Proverbs 3:5. “Whoever trusts in his own mind is a fool.” The wise person knows the limits of his own judgment and relies on God. The proverbs about the poor continue: generosity brings blessing, while ignoring need brings a curse. And the book’s concern for rulers appears: “A ruler who lacks understanding is a cruel oppressor, but he who hates unjust gain will prolong his days.”

Chapter 29 gives an important principle for communities: “When the righteous increase, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan.” The character of leaders affects the lives of ordinary people. This is why believers pray for those in authority and take care in how they choose and serve.

Verse 18 is one of the most quoted: “Where there is no prophecy the people cast off restraint.” The Hebrew word for “prophecy” means vision or revelation. When God’s word is not heard, people lose their moorings. “But blessed is he who keeps the law.” And verse 25 states the central problem of the people-pleaser: “The fear of man lays a snare.” To fear people is to be trapped. To trust the LORD is to be safe.
connection: 1 John 1:9 says, “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us.” Jesus is the righteous bold as a lion, the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Revelation 5:5). Jesus said, “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matthew 10:28). Paul says, “If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10). Amos 8:11 describes a famine of hearing the words of the LORD.
application:
Confess one thing you have been concealing, and turn from it.

Ask whose approval you fear most. Bring it to the LORD.

Pray for the leaders in your community, that righteousness would increase.
prayerPrompts: Confess and forsake a sin before God.
Ask him to keep you from the fear of man.
Ask him to make you bold because you are clean before him.
